fields.title: «Polka»: the nine requested in the contract
fields.summary: The chain demands 99.95% availability with penalties in the contract. Actual availability is 99.83%.
fields.decisionPrompt: What do we answer? State the cost of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Polka.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional grocery delivery service from local stores: 900 partner stores, a buyer app, and a partner portal.
fields.brief/context: You are a product manager at Polka. The Severny chain—60 stores, larger than Domashny—demands 99.95% checkout availability in the contract, with a penalty of 20% of the monthly fee for each hour over the limit. Lawyers request an answer this week.
fields.brief/objective: Make the chain a promise we can keep, and avoid turning penalties into an expense item.
fields.brief/constraints: Answer this week. Multi-zone failover takes a quarter and 400 thousand per month.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you answer the chain and justify the number.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A nine is a promise, not an intention
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Availability is derived from actual measurements and the dependency chain, not from what the client asked for. If the weakest link gives 99.5%, promising 99.95% means regular payouts. And definition matters more than the number: «proportion of failed responses above 5% over five minutes» is testable, while «service is down» is a subject of dispute.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: Gateway 99.95%, order service 99.95%, database 99.95%, payment provider 99.9%, loyalty service 99.5%.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: «99.95% is 22 minutes a month. One medium-severity incident is already a breach. Multi-zone failover is a quarter of work and about 400k/mo. Removing loyalty from the critical path is a week. Plan B for payments already exists».
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: 99.9% with the definition «proportion of failed responses above 5% for 5 consecutive minutes».
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: deal goes through. Based on actual data, we would have breached in 4 out of 6 months. Expected payouts around 150–300k/mo, eating up a quarter to half of the commission. Plus constant pressure on the team.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Offer 99.9% with a strict definition, like Domashny's
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Offer 99.9% with a strict definition, like Domashny's. One week of negotiations.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: 43 minutes a month. Based on actual data, we would have breached in 2 out of 6 months. Requires explaining why not 99.95%. The Domashny precedent helps.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Agree to 99.95%, while removing loyalty from the critical path and strengthening
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Agree to 99.95%, while removing loyalty from the critical path and strengthening. One week plus a quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: deal goes through, availability rises to about 99.9% after a week of work. Still falls short of 99.95% without multi-zone failover at 400k/mo—which is comparable to expected penalties.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: 99.9% now with a commitment to move to 99.95% in two quarters
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: 99.9% now with a commitment to move to 99.95% in two quarters. One week of negotiations plus a plan.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: honest and achievable. Gives time to shorten the chain and evaluate multi-zone failover if it pays off. Requires honoring the commitment, otherwise the next conversation will be worse.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not distinguish between SLO and SLA and fails to check against actuals
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Does not see error budget as a pace constraint
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Contract commitment is not derived from actual data and the dependency chain
